case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging yellow-red plaque on his chest that was accompanied by mild pain. The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging yellow-red plaque on his chest that was accompanied by mild pain. The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging yellow-red plaque on his chest that was accompanied by mild pain. The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions.
